query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Mo with a lower electronegativity, more ductility‐promoting element (such as V) in the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy will reduce the overall electronegativity mismatch without heavily compromising the solid solution strengthening, thereby improving plasticity under room-temperature compression while largely maintaining high yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, a disordered BCC solid solution exhibiting a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa but limited ductility due to the high Mo content.
generation.intervention: Replace a portion (e.g., 10–20 atomic percent) of Mo with V to form a modified alloy composition NbZrTiHfMo(1–x)Vx.
generation.conditions: Samples are produced by arc melting (or similar high-temperature melting) and homogenization annealing. The alloys will be tested under room-temperature quasi‐static compression with standard loading rates to measure yield strength and ductility.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified lattice distortion and reduced electronegativity difference in the BCC solid solution.
generation.mechanism: Substituting Mo with V lowers the overall electronegativity mismatch among the constituent elements. This reduction diminishes directional bonding and promotes enhanced dislocation mobility (i.e. easier slip), thereby increasing plasticity. At the same time, the remaining refractory elements preserve much of the solid solution strengthening, keeping the yield strength high.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in room-temperature ductility (plastic strain) relative to the baseline NbZrTiHfMo alloy while maintaining a yield strength near or only slightly below 1719 MPa, within the limits of a modest (<20 at%) Mo reduction.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo showing high compressive yield strength (~1719 MPa) but reduced plasticity due to the high Mo content.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected only for modest substitutions (up to about 20 at% replacement of Mo); higher substitution levels might excessively reduce strength by weakening solid solution strengthening contributions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal substitution level and the precise balance of strength versus plasticity remain uncertain until validated experimentally, as processing history and microstructural homogeneity could also influence outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys with V substituting for Mo at levels of 0%, 10%, and 20% using arc melting followed by homogenization annealing to ensure a uniform disordered BCC structure. Perform room-temperature quasi-static compression tests to determine compressive yield strength and plastic strain. Complement these tests with phase analysis (XRD) and microstructural observations (SEM/TEM) to verify that no deleterious phases are precipitated.
measurements: XRD to assess phase stability and lattice parameters
TEM/SEM for dislocation structures and homogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the V-substituted alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement in ductility (e.g., an increase of at least 10–15% in plastic strain) compared to the baseline NbZrTiHfMo alloy, or if there is a severe drop in yield strength (e.g., below ~1600 MPa), indicating that the intervention does not preserve the required strength.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
